A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MCU and retain its foundation of composable Minecraft atomic tasks, despite v2's changed title and substantial revision. All pages, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original data analyses: task-space clustering using difficulty features and comparisons of benchmark difficulty distributions (Section 4; Figures 3–4). These qualify even though v1 lacks direct agent-performance experiments.

after.justification: V2 reports original agent rollouts, human assessments, automated-evaluator comparisons, difficulty experiments and annotated task profiles (Section 4; Appendices D–G).

M1.justification: The composable-task foundation remains, but v2 adds an automated procedure: GPT-4o generates randomized executable environments, Mineflayer verifies tasks and provides revision feedback, and a VLM scores videos using generated task-specific criteria (Section 3). These are substantive new components beyond v1's task construction, difficulty scoring and benchmark filtering.

E1.justification: Minecraft and many atomic goals are retained. V2 adds a trajectory-assessment dataset covering 60 tasks and over 500 human/agent videos, plus agent evaluations on 30 atomic and five compositional tasks under varied initial states and distracting conditions (Section 4). These introduce new evaluated data and task requirements beyond v1's task-list and difficulty analyses.

E2.justification: V1 mentions MineCLIP as a possible metric and surveys prior agents' task lists without corresponding performance comparisons. V2 evaluates its scorer against MineCLIP and a version without generated criteria (Table 2), and introduces comparisons among VPT-bc, VPT-rl, STEVE-1 and GROOT, with human reference performance in Figures 9–10.

E3.justification: V1's six difficulty axes combine trajectory measurements, graph complexity and human ratings. V2 uses five human-rated axes, adding visual diversity and omitting operational effort and planning complexity (Appendix D). It also introduces paired and individual video-rating protocols, F1/Kendall/TrueSkill metrics, three difficulty levels and task-specific success definitions (Section 4; Appendix F).

E4.justification: V1's task-clustering and benchmark-difficulty-bias analyses are removed. V2 adds an ablation testing generated evaluation criteria (Table 2), robustness tests examining harder initial conditions and distractions (Figure 6; Table 5), and detailed pillar-building and snow-golem evaluation cases (Appendix G.8). These address substantially different diagnostic questions.

E5.justification: V2 introduces explicit replication and uncertainty reporting: ten rollouts per task/difficulty, averages from at least three human annotations, named world seeds, Kendall's tau with a p-value, and Gaussian TrueSkill uncertainty with plotted error bars (Section 4; Appendices E–F; Figure 10). V1 has no comparable reporting. This does not establish increased runs for any retained experiment.

E6.justification: V1's clustering and benchmark-distribution results disappear. V2 adds evaluator results: Table 2 reports average F1 of 80.0 with criteria, 73.0 without criteria and 44.0 for MineCLIP; Table 3 reports 90.8 across dimensions. It also adds agent rankings led by GROOT in Table 4 and difficulty-dependent success rates in Figure 6. These are new experiments, without matching performance results in v1.

T1.justification: V2 removes the mathematical task-difficulty construction: v1's E+V planning approximation, permutation-entropy formulation and claimed independence from sequence length, and piecewise quantile calibration to [0,5] (Section 3; Appendices A and C). V2 instead introduces goal-conditioned initial-state and stratified-sampling formulations (Section 3.2; Appendix E). Neither version supplies a theorem-and-proof development.

C1.justification: Composable tasks remain central, but v1's headline contributions of six-dimensional task space, SkillForge and targeted filtering are replaced by claims of fully automated generation, verification and evaluation. V2 additionally claims over 90% agreement with human assessment and experimentally demonstrated limitations of foundation agents under greater task diversity and difficulty (abstract, introduction and conclusion).

C2.justification: V1 interprets task distributions as revealing benchmark bias and guiding representative task selection. V2 adds explanations involving inventory distractions, dependence on demonstration locations, and increased material-use scores from redundant items (Section 4.2.3). It also identifies limitations of video subsampling for detailed crafting judgments (Section 4.1), substantially expanding mechanism and failure-condition discussion.

D1.justification: V2 adds Minecraft version, frame rate, observation/action specifications, inventory-generation procedures, human-video collection details, task success metrics, full prompts and verification/evaluation pseudocode (Appendices B–G). These substantially expand implementation documentation. Conversely, v1's explicit MCU repository link is omitted, and v2 describes annotated tasks as a future release; this establishes changed access information, not repository unavailability.

R1.justification: V1 concentrates on Minecraft task coverage and MineDojo's shortcomings. V2 substantially broadens positioning to generalist-agent benchmarks, including DmLab, Procgen, Crafter, Xland and DYVAL (Table 1), and adds BEDD and LLM-as-judge research (Section 5). Appendix G also compares prior systems' observation/action simplifications, reshaping the rationale for MCU.

P1.justification: V2 retitles the paper, changes the author information and extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction and conclusion. The narrative moves from atom/molecule tasks, difficulty scores and task-space analysis to benchmark desiderata, an automated pipeline and empirical validation. The appendices are extensively reorganized and rewritten, beyond changes caused solely by adding experiments.

P2.justification: V1's taxonomy, dependency graph, t-SNE visualization, benchmark-distribution radars and text-interface screenshot give way to automation diagrams, evaluator/agent performance charts, difficulty comparisons and rating-interface screenshots. V2 also introduces five-axis per-task radar charts, expanded tables and formatted prompt/code listings. This substantially changes the visual presentation rather than merely renumbering displays.

improvement.justification: V2 closes an important practical validation gap: v1 proposes an evaluation framework without direct agent benchmarking or validation against human judgments. V2 adds human validation, a MineCLIP comparison, a criteria ablation and repeated difficulty-controlled agent trials, supported by much fuller implementation documentation. Losing the task-space analyses and project link is a drawback, and reporting issues remain, including broad agreement wording and Table 5's inconsistent efficiency delta. Nevertheless, the new methodological and empirical support substantially improves the paper's overall quality.
